Name: Adam
Transcript: Thanks for having me. There are no right answers, it's your experience I'm after, and we can stop at any point. So, to begin. Can you tell me what it's like, sharing your home with a dog?

Name: Mabel
Transcript: Well. It's noisy, for a start. No, I'm teasing. Pepper. She's a springer, mostly, there's something else in there nobody's owned up to. She's two and a half. And what's it like. It's like having the lights on. That's the nearest I can get to it. After Dennis died the house was, everything stayed where I'd left it. You'd put a cup down and it would still be there in the morning. And now nothing's where I left it. My slippers are in the garden, there's a tennis ball in the bread bin, I don't know how. And I wouldn't swap it.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Nothing's where you left it.

Name: Mabel
Transcript: No. And I'm a tidy person, or I was. Dennis used to say I'd have the plates cleared before he'd finished. So it's a funny thing to be glad of. But a house where things stay put is a house where nothing's happening. I had two years of that and I don't want it back. I like coming in and finding she's carried my glasses case into her bed. It means somebody's been living here.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Can you take me through an ordinary day with her?

Name: Mabel
Transcript: She gets me up at seven. She doesn't bark, she's very polite, she comes and sits by the bed and stares at me. You can feel it through your eyelids. And if I don't stir she puts her chin on the mattress. So I get up. Before her I'd lie there till nine some days, there wasn't anything to get up for. I'd retired, Dennis had gone, I'd just lie there with the radio on. Now it's seven o'clock, dressing gown, kettle on, let her out, and we're on the green by half past. Rain or shine. I've got waterproof trousers now. I'd never owned waterproof trousers in my life.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What's the green like at half past seven?

Name: Mabel
Transcript: Oh, it's a whole society. You wouldn't know it unless you had a dog. There's the same six or seven of us most mornings, and we stand by the bench while they all run about, and we talk. I didn't know any of these people three years ago. I'd lived on this estate twenty years and I didn't know them. There's Terry with his two greyhounds, he was a postman, and there's a young girl with a little dachshund who's a nurse and comes off nights half asleep. And I know all the dogs' names and about half the people's. That's the etiquette. The dogs first.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What's it like, being part of that?

Name: Mabel
Transcript: It's lovely. I don't want to overdo it, but it's saved me a bit. When Dennis was ill I stopped seeing people, there wasn't the time, and then after, I'd lost the habit. You forget how. And with a dog you don't need to know how, because you're not there to see people, you're there for the dog, and the talking just happens round the edges. Nobody has to make an effort. When Terry's knee was bad I took his greyhounds round with Pepper for a fortnight. Three dogs. I looked like I was being pulled along by a sled team.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You said it's saved you a bit.

Name: Mabel
Transcript: Did I? Well. Yes. I'm not one for big words. But I was in a bad way that second winter on my own. I wasn't eating properly. I'd have toast for my tea most nights, standing up at the counter. My daughter was worried, she rang every day, and I'd say I was fine, and I wasn't. And now I've got to be up and out and someone's depending on me, and you can't feed a dog and not feed yourself, it looks ridiculous. So I eat. I sit down to it. Pepper sits next to me waiting for crusts.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Has it always been easy, having her?

Name: Mabel
Transcript: No. Oh, no. The first six months I thought I'd made a terrible mistake. She chewed everything. She ate the corner off the kitchen cupboard. She ate a whole loaf once, bag and all. And she pulled. My goodness, she pulled. I'm seventy three, I'm not built for it. And then last January there was ice on the path by the shops and a cat came out from under a car, and she went, and I went with her. Flat on my face. Broke my wrist.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What happened after that?

Name: Mabel
Transcript: Well, my daughter came down, and she was very upset, and in the car on the way back from the hospital she said, Mum, the dog has to go. Just like that. And I said, she does not. And we didn't speak for most of the way home. It's the only proper row we've had in years. She thought she was looking after me, and she was, I know she was. But it felt like she was taking something off me. Like I was a child who'd been given a puppy and couldn't be trusted with it.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What was that like, being spoken to like that?

Name: Mabel
Transcript: I felt small. And frightened too, if I'm honest, because she had a point, hadn't she. I'd broken my wrist. I lay in bed that night with my arm in a sling and Pepper on the floor beside me, she wasn't allowed on the bed then, and I thought, what if it had been my hip. What happens to her then. What happens to me. I didn't sleep much. But I knew I wasn't giving her up. I knew that by the morning.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What did you do?

Name: Mabel
Transcript: I took her to classes. At my age! The church hall on a Tuesday night, all these young couples with their puppies, and me with my wrist in plaster. And a harness, a proper one that clips at the front so she can't get her shoulders into it. And I learned to stop when she pulls. Just stop dead and stand there like a lamppost until she comes back. It takes forever. The first week it took us forty minutes to get to the end of the road. But she learned. She walks nicely now, mostly. Not when there's a cat.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And how are things with your daughter now?

Name: Mabel
Transcript: Better. She came to watch a class in the end. She stood at the back with her arms folded, and by the end she was laughing, because Pepper did a perfect sit and then lay down and rolled over without being asked. Showing off. And afterwards she said, all right, Mum. That was all. All right. And I knew what she meant. We've not talked about it since, really. But she brings Pepper a chew when she comes now. That's how I know.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You said you wondered what would happen to Pepper. Is that something you think about?

Name: Mabel
Transcript: All the time. Not in a gloomy way. Well, sometimes in a gloomy way. But mostly practical. I'm seventy three and she's two and a half, and springers can go fifteen years. You do the sums. She could well outlive me. So I've sorted it. Terry's niece, who's got a spaniel herself, has said she'll have her. It's in writing. It's with the solicitor, with my will. My daughter thought that was morbid. I think it's the most responsible thing I've ever done.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Sorry, Terry's niece?

Name: Mabel
Transcript: Yes, his niece, Carol. She's on the green some Sundays.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What was it like, sorting that out?

Name: Mabel
Transcript: Strange. Sitting in the solicitor's office with Pepper's name on a piece of paper, next to the house and Dennis's watch. Who gets what. He didn't bat an eyelid, he said he does a lot of pets now. But I came out and sat on the wall outside and I felt lighter. Like I'd put something down. Because it had been sitting with me, the not knowing, every time she looked at me. And now if anything happens she won't be left in an empty house waiting. That was the picture I couldn't stand. Her waiting by the door for me.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Her waiting by the door.

Name: Mabel
Transcript: Yes. Because she does, you see. When I go to the shops she's at the window when I come back. Every time. The man next door says she sits there the whole time I'm out. And I couldn't bear the thought of her doing that and me never coming. So that's done now. I don't think about my own end much, I never have, Dennis was the worrier. But I think about her being all right after it. That's the bit I needed settled.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Does she ever bring Dennis to mind?

Name: Mabel
Transcript: Oh, she never knew him. She came two years after. But yes. In the evenings. I talk to her, and I find I'm telling her the things I'd have told him. What I saw at the shops, who said what on the green, what the doctor said about my wrist. Daft things. She listens beautifully, she tips her head. And sometimes I catch myself and think, Mabel, you're telling a dog the price of butter. But it's a habit of forty years, telling someone about your day. It had nowhere to go. Now it goes to her.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Where does she sleep?

Name: Mabel
Transcript: Well. That's a sore point with my daughter. She's on the bed now. On his side. It started after the wrist, I couldn't get down to her on the floor, and she just got up one night and lay down and that was that. I know what people would say. I know what my daughter says, she says it's not hygienic. But it's nice to hear breathing. I'll say that and leave it there. It's nice to hear breathing in the night again.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Is there anything else about living with her that we haven't touched on?

Name: Mabel
Transcript: Only that I didn't expect it. Any of it. I got her because the house was too quiet and I thought a dog would be some noise. I didn't expect the green, or Terry, or the classes, or the solicitor. I didn't expect to be fitter at seventy three than I was at sixty. She opened the door, really, that's what it is. I was shut in and she opened the door. Some mornings I'd still rather she hadn't, when it's sleeting. But mostly I'm glad. I'm very glad.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Thank you, Mabel. That's really helpful. I'll stop the recording there.

Name: Mabel
Transcript: Is that it? Oh, that went quickly. Will you have a biscuit before you go?
